claims.text: Heating sub-10 nm equiatomic Au-Co-Cu-Ni-Pt nanoparticles to 1000 K causes structural evolution dominated by surface-energy-driven segregation and rapid phase separation rather than sluggish diffusion.
In sub-10 nm particles, surface diffusion coefficients are orders of magnitude higher than bulk diffusion coefficients.
Au-Co and Au-Pt pairs have strong negative mixing enthalpies.
The mixing enthalpies of Au-Co and Au-Pt overcome configurational-entropy stabilization and drive segregation.
The smallest particles disappear through Ostwald ripening accelerated by fast surface diffusion.
Particle faceting or coalescence is driven by surface-energy minimization and segregated-phase formation.
The initial nanoparticles are likely metastable solid solutions or partially ordered states.
Au and Pt are low-surface-energy elements that segregate to the particle exterior.
Co, Cu, and Ni diffuse inward to form segregated cores or intermetallic precipitates.
In sub-10 nm nanoparticles, surface diffusion dominates bulk diffusion.
Sufficiently negative mixing enthalpy can overcome entropy stabilization and lead to intermetallic-compound formation in equiatomic high-entropy alloys.
The sluggish-diffusion effect reported for bulk high-entropy alloys becomes negligible in these nanoparticles because surface kinetics dominate.
Au/Pt-rich shells and Co/Cu/Ni-rich cores or intermetallic precipitates form within the first few minutes of heating.
Heating significantly reduces the number of particles smaller than 5 nm.
Particles evolve from spherical shapes to faceted or irregular shapes during heating.
The final material is multiphase and chemically segregated rather than a single-phase solid solution.
High configurational entropy and sluggish diffusion can enhance the thermal stability of high-entropy alloys.
The proposed mechanism applies below 10 nm, whereas bulk diffusion may dominate above 50 nm and sluggish diffusion may re-emerge.
Vacuum prevents oxidation, ensuring that the observed changes are intrinsic to the alloy.
Absence of detectable segregation and Ostwald ripening after heating to 1000 K would falsify the hypothesis.

contradictions.description: The same strong negative mixing enthalpy is invoked both as the driver of compositional phase separation and as the driver of intermetallic formation. These distinct outcomes are presented interchangeably without explaining which thermodynamic pathway is expected or under what conditions each occurs.
